sentences.text: Pujatopouli is known from a partially preserved skull and postcranial elements, making it one of the most complete Mesozoic crown group birds.
It weighed up to 2.03 kg, which is smaller than the contemporary bird Polarornis.
The beak was long, narrow, straight and pointed, unlike the rounded beaks of early galloanserine birds.
The genus was formally described in 2026 by Facundo Irazoqui and colleagues.
The name combines the surname of Hernán Pujato with the Greek word for bird, while the species epithet honors the Argentine military group Patrulla Soberanía.
Pujatopouli likely hunted small invertebrates and fish by diving using its feet, a strategy comparable to that of modern diving birds.
It is placed within the extinct genus of neoavian birds.
Phylogenetic analyses suggest it belongs to the clade Aequornithes and is a sister taxon to the family Procellaridae.
Pujatopouli lived during the Maastrichtian stage of the Late Cretaceous, between 72.2 and 66 million years ago.
Some researchers question whether Pujatopouli can be securely assigned to Neoaves, despite its apparent affinities with Aequornithes.
